script: People are way too uptight about their dogs now.. I woke up to the sound of my dog digging a hole in the yard, the earth shaking under his paws like a drumbeat. The sun was just creeping over the horizon, and I could hear the faint rustle of leaves—classic morning chaos. But here's the thing… the dog didn't care that I was still half asleep, he was already in full‑blown excavation mode. What I didn't know was that this tiny act would ignite a whole saga of judgment from the neighborhood. Fast‑forward to the 2000s, and I was a kid with a backyard full of pups who could run wild, chase squirrels, and bark at anything that dared cross their path. Obedience training was the bare minimum—"sit," "stay," and "no begging" were the only commands on the menu. However… the world had shifted, and now people expect every dog to get four 30‑minute walks, a curated diet, and weekend "adventures" that sound like a marketing ploy. And that's when everything changed—my childhood freedom became a lesson in hypocrisy. Working at a dog daycare, I've seen the same people who scream abuse when a pup doesn't meet their "perfect" standards. They board their dogs for 2–3 weeks while family stays at home, but when the dog is at the daycare, the environment is loud, overstimulated, and every routine is a test. Until… I realized that even in a top‑tier facility, the stress level can be off the charts. If this didn't work, I'd lose every single happy tail in the world. My own dog? He lives like a king. A huge yard where he can go in and out whenever he wants, endless toys, high‑quality kibble, occasional table scraps, and an underground fence that he respects like a sacred boundary. The worst thing we have? A fence. But here's the thing… he sleeps on a couch that costs more than my mattress, and he still digs holes like a rebel. What I didn't know was that some people would see this as a crime. People say you shouldn't get a dog unless you can "give them the life they deserve." Is that a threat or a joke? The audacity of that statement is that they define "life" as a concrete sidewalk and a treadmill. However… I let my dog chase deer and raccoons, he can run around like a kid, and I use only positive reinforcement. And that's when everything changed—my dog is thriving, and so is my sanity. When I mention that my dog can dig holes or try some of my food, the judgment hits like a punch. "You can't let him do that!" they hiss, as if the dog is a menace. But here's the thing… he is a dog, not a pet; he should be allowed to do dog things, and I am the best bestie who knows how to keep him safe and happy. What I didn't know was that the real problem lies with people who can't handle their own anxiety and project it onto animals. In the end, if you think I am letting my dog run wild, you're just missing the point. I give him a life that's all about freedom, love, and responsibility. This wasn't just about a pet; it was about setting standards that respect both the animal and the owner. And that's the tea—my dog gets the life he deserves, and I am still the best friend in the room.
